Sí, ese método sirve, pero no debería ser el único.

Entrenar con datos antiguos y evaluar en el bloque más reciente no usado es una muy buena idea como test final intocable porque respeta la flecha temporal. El problema es que, si lo usas solo, tu resultado queda demasiado atado a un solo régimen de mercado, un solo corte temporal y una sola muestra reciente. Para este proyecto, tu propia documentación ya empuja hacia una evaluación time-aware con walk-forward, además de purge/embargo por horizontes solapados, y también contempla métricas de regresión, clasificación y ranking, más ablaciones.

Mi opinión: la mejor solución casi nunca es “solo holdout reciente”. La solución más fuerte suele ser:

  • walk-forward como evaluación principal,

  • purge/embargo para evitar contaminación entre horizontes,

  • un bloque final reciente totalmente intocable como “lockbox test”,

  • y comparación con varias formulaciones de benchmark, incluyendo ranking y targets ajustados cuando aplique.

Te dejo un prompt mucho más fuerte, pensado para usarlo en Deep Research o con otro modelo, y alineado con tu proyecto:

You are acting as a rigorous research auditor and benchmarking strategist for a Master’s-level financial machine learning project.

Your task is to investigate, compare, critique, and recommend the best possible benchmarking methodology for my model.

This is NOT a trading-bot benchmarking task.
This is NOT an intraday or high-frequency task.
This IS an academic, end-of-day, multimodal, multi-horizon forecasting project that must be:
- leakage-aware,
- reproducible,
- methodologically defensible,
- and strong enough for thesis-level evaluation.

CRITICAL RULES
1. Do NOT hallucinate.
   - If any claim about benchmarking methodology, literature, validation design, metric choice, statistical test, leakage mitigation, or common financial-ML benchmarking practice is uncertain, say:
     “Uncertain, verify manually.”
   - Then propose a concrete verification step.
2. Separate clearly:
   - Established findings
   - Plausible methodological recommendations
   - Speculative ideas that require testing
3. Do not present guesses as facts.
4. Prefer primary or highly credible sources when possible.
5. Be critical, not agreeable.
6. Accuracy is the main priority, but robustness, leakage safety, and scientific defensibility are also critical.
7. If two benchmarking strategies seem similar in predictive usefulness, prefer the one that is:
   - less leak-prone,
   - more reproducible,
   - more stable across market regimes,
   - easier to defend academically.

PROJECT CONTEXT YOU MUST ASSUME
Use the following as current project reality unless I explicitly override it:

- This is an end-of-day, multimodal, multi-horizon financial forecasting system.
- The hypothesis is that an aggregated recent-news “event state” can improve prediction over market-only baselines.
- Market data is daily OHLCV.
- News is timestamped and must obey strict as-of-close alignment.
- Horizons are primarily 1 day, 5 days, 20 days, and optionally 60 days.
- The project is not trying to predict raw price level.
- It is closer to:
  - return prediction,
  - abnormal/excess return prediction,
  - direction prediction,
  - downside-risk prediction,
  - and possibly uncertainty-aware outputs.
- The evaluation must be leakage-aware.
- Walk-forward, purge, and embargo are already considered important in the current project logic.
- The project may use regression metrics, classification metrics, ranking metrics, and ablations.
- The benchmarking methodology must be appropriate for:
  - temporal dependence,
  - overlapping horizons,
  - non-stationarity,
  - regime shifts,
  - and financial noise.

MY INITIAL IDEA THAT YOU MUST EVALUATE
My current idea is something like this:
- train the model using data up to a certain point in time,
- then evaluate on the most recent data that was never used during training.

I want you to assess this idea critically:
- Is it good?
- When is it useful?
- What are its weaknesses?
- Is it enough by itself?
- What types of bias or instability can remain even if it is temporally valid?
- Should it be used as:
  - the main benchmark,
  - only the final untouched holdout,
  - or just one piece of a broader evaluation protocol?

PRIMARY OBJECTIVE
I want a full deep-research investigation into the best ways to benchmark this type of model.

Your job is to determine:
1. what benchmarking strategies exist for this kind of project,
2. which ones are strongest scientifically,
3. which ones are strongest for real predictive assessment,
4. which ones are dangerous or misleading,
5. and what final benchmarking framework I should adopt.

I want your answer to be very long, deeply structured, and highly critical.

REQUIRED OUTPUT STRUCTURE

SECTION 1 — Restate the Benchmarking Problem in Research Terms
Please restate the problem as an academic benchmarking question for:
- end-of-day forecasting,
- multi-horizon labels,
- multimodal inputs,
- noisy financial targets,
- and strict temporal causality.

Clarify:
- what is being benchmarked,
- what is not being benchmarked,
- what “good benchmarking” means in this context,
- why naive train/test thinking is often insufficient in financial ML,
- and why leakage-aware temporal design is mandatory.

SECTION 2 — Evaluate My Proposed Method
Critically analyze this method:
- train on older data,
- test on the most recent unseen data.

I want you to discuss:
1. why it is a reasonable starting point,
2. what it captures well,
3. what it fails to capture,
4. how sensitive it is to regime dependence,
5. whether it wastes valuable time variation,
6. whether it is statistically fragile,
7. whether it is enough as the only reported benchmark,
8. whether it is better suited as:
   - main validation,
   - final holdout,
   - sanity check,
   - or one component inside a larger framework.

SECTION 3 — Enumerate the Main Benchmarking Families
Investigate and explain the major benchmarking/evaluation strategies relevant to this project, including at minimum:
1. single chronological holdout
2. rolling walk-forward validation
3. expanding-window walk-forward validation
4. rolling-origin evaluation
5. purged and embargoed temporal cross-validation
6. combinatorial purged cross-validation if relevant
7. nested time-series validation for model selection vs final assessment
8. final locked recent holdout / lockbox test

For each one, explain:
- what it is,
- how it works conceptually,
- what scientific question it answers,
- what kinds of leakage or bias it helps avoid,
- what its weaknesses are,
- and how suitable it is for:
  - 1d horizons,
  - 5d horizons,
  - 20d horizons,
  - 60d horizons.

SECTION 4 — Financial-ML-Specific Benchmarking Risks
I want a prioritized analysis of the main dangers that can make benchmarking misleading in this type of project.

At minimum include:
1. look-ahead bias
2. overlapping-label contamination
3. leakage through feature normalization
4. leakage through text alignment / after-hours news
5. survivorship bias
6. benchmark contamination through universe design
7. regime-specific lucky test periods
8. selection bias from trying many experiments
9. backtest overfitting
10. metric cherry-picking
11. calibration blindness
12. evaluating only one horizon and generalizing conclusions
13. evaluating only one market regime
14. corporate actions contamination if labels rely on bad prices
15. misuse of the newest block as both validation and test

For each risk, explain:
- why it matters,
- how it distorts conclusions,
- how it can be detected,
- how it should be prevented.

SECTION 5 — Metrics and What They Really Measure
Investigate what metrics should be reported in benchmarking this model.

Discuss and compare:
Regression metrics:
- MAE
- RMSE
- R²
- Pearson correlation
- Spearman correlation

Classification metrics:
- Accuracy
- Balanced accuracy
- AUC
- PR-AUC
- Brier score

Ranking metrics:
- Information Coefficient
- ICIR
- cross-sectional rank correlation
- top-k hit rate

Probabilistic / uncertainty metrics if relevant:
- calibration curves
- proper scoring rules
- quantile-related metrics
- probabilistic sharpness vs calibration

For each metric family, explain:
- what it captures,
- what it misses,
- how it can be misleading,
- and which ones are most appropriate for this exact project.

SECTION 6 — What Should Be the True Primary Benchmark Objective?
I want you to analyze what the project should truly optimize and benchmark around:
- raw returns,
- abnormal/excess returns,
- direction,
- downside risk,
- ranking,
- probabilistic confidence,
- or some combination.

Discuss whether:
- ranking is more defensible than point prediction,
- abnormal returns are stronger than raw returns,
- horizon-specific benchmarking should dominate aggregate benchmarking,
- and whether a model can look weak on RMSE but still be genuinely useful on ranking.

SECTION 7 — Tournament of 8 Benchmarking Strategies
This section is mandatory.

Construct a tournament-style comparison of at least 8 serious benchmarking strategies for this project.

These 8 strategies must be meaningfully different, for example:
1. single recent chronological holdout
2. rolling walk-forward only
3. expanding-window walk-forward only
4. walk-forward + purge/embargo
5. walk-forward + final lockbox holdout
6. nested temporal validation + final lockbox
7. cross-sectional ranking-focused benchmark design
8. multi-objective benchmark design combining regression + ranking + calibration

You may rename/refine these if better alternatives exist, but there must be at least 8.

For each candidate strategy, evaluate:
- expected realism
- expected leakage safety
- expected statistical stability
- expected fairness
- expected computational cost
- expected interpretability
- suitability for thesis defense
- suitability for model selection
- suitability for final reporting
- suitability under limited data
- suitability under regime shifts

Tournament rules:
- Arrange them in a bracket / elimination / tournament-style structure.
- In each matchup, explicitly state which strategy wins and why.
- Accuracy quality is the primary criterion.
- If predictive-evaluation quality seems similar, prefer:
  - cleaner methodology,
  - stronger leakage protection,
  - better reproducibility,
  - stronger thesis defensibility.
- At the end, report:
  - overall winner,
  - runner-up,
  - best low-risk/high-confidence strategy,
  - best high-risk/high-reward strategy,
  - best strategy if the thesis must stay narrow,
  - best strategy if I can afford a more elaborate evaluation protocol.

SECTION 8 — Best Final Benchmarking Architecture
Based on the tournament, recommend the best overall benchmarking framework for this project.

I want a concrete methodological recommendation answering:
- What should be the main validation protocol?
- What should be the final untouched test protocol?
- What should be used for model selection?
- What should be used for ablations?
- What should be used for final thesis tables and figures?
- What should be used for robustness checks?

Be explicit about:
- which parts are “must do”,
- which parts are “strongly recommended”,
- which parts are optional.

SECTION 9 — Unified Strategy Discussion
I want you to discuss whether the strongest benchmarking strategies can be combined into one single evaluation framework.

Specifically discuss:
1. whether combining strategies is possible,
2. whether combining them is scientifically wise,
3. whether it improves confidence,
4. whether it makes the protocol too complex,
5. whether it creates reporting confusion,
6. whether it increases computational burden too much,
7. whether it makes hyperparameter tuning cleaner or dirtier,
8. whether it improves robustness to regime shifts,
9. whether it makes the thesis more defensible,
10. whether it risks becoming overengineered.

Then discuss clearly the:
Advantages of combining strategies:
- better robustness,
- better regime coverage,
- better separation of validation vs final test,
- better confidence in conclusions,
- better ablation discipline,
- stronger thesis defense.

Disadvantages of combining strategies:
- complexity,
- harder interpretation,
- more opportunities for selection bias,
- heavier computation,
- harder narrative,
- greater risk of accidental protocol misuse.

Then give a verdict:
- Should I combine strategies?
- If yes, which combination is best?
- If not, what simpler protocol is best?

SECTION 10 — Final Recommendation and Brutally Honest Verdict
End with direct answers to all of the following:
1. Is my original idea good?
2. Is it enough by itself?
3. What is the best primary benchmarking method?
4. What is the best final holdout method?
5. What is the best overall strategy for this thesis?
6. What is the most dangerous benchmarking mistake I could make next?
7. What should I absolutely not do?
8. If I want the strongest academically defensible evaluation, what exact philosophy should guide me?

OUTPUT REQUIREMENTS
Your answer must be:
- very long,
- deeply structured,
- critical,
- explicit,
- not generic,
- honest about uncertainty,
- focused on theory and methodology,
- suitable for a Master’s thesis context,
- and careful about financial-ML-specific pitfalls.

SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS
- Do not hallucinate.
- If uncertain, say so explicitly and propose how to verify.
- If my original approach is incomplete, say so directly.
- If a strategy is common but weak, say so.
- If a strategy is strong but too expensive/complex, say so.
- If the best answer is a hybrid protocol, explain exactly why.
- If the best answer depends on whether I optimize for thesis clarity vs maximum robustness, explain both cases separately.
- Be willing to conclude that a simpler but cleaner strategy is better than a more elaborate but fragile one.

Now perform the full benchmarking-methodology investigation.

Si quieres, después te hago una segunda versión todavía más agresiva y más larga, especializada para Deep Research, con más énfasis en literatura académica, pruebas estadísticas y benchmarking para series financieras.

At the repository/planning level, the project is currently framed as an end-of-day, multimodal, multi-horizon financial forecasting system built around market data, a news-derived event-state representation, and optional company/profile/context branches; it is explicitly not framed as a trading bot, an intraday system, or a price-level predictor. 1. Executive summary

The project is now best understood as a research program on whether a temporally aggregated “event state” derived from recent financial news can improve multi-horizon stock forecasting beyond market-only baselines, under a strict end-of-day, leakage-aware evaluation framework. The most important practical conclusion from the current research state is that the project is no longer just about “building a model”; it is about building a scientifically defensible forecasting pipeline whose value depends as much on target definition, data alignment, split handling, and benchmarking discipline as on architecture choice. That conclusion is consistent both with the project’s own current framing and with the broader multimodal-finance literature, which repeatedly highlights temporal misalignment, modality imbalance, noisy labels, and weak evaluation discipline as major reasons why apparently strong multimodal systems fail to generalize. In practical terms, the project’s present theoretical center of gravity is this:

  • Target: returns / abnormal returns / direction / downside risk, rather than raw price levels.

  • Core modalities: daily OHLCV + timestamped financial news.

  • Core representation hypothesis: recent news should be treated as an evolving contextual state, not as isolated one-article-one-impact events.

  • Core evaluation requirement: walk-forward, temporally causal, overlap-aware benchmarking with a final untouched recent holdout.

  • Core tension: whether the next gains come from richer architecture, richer data, or cleaner targets and cleaner evaluation.

  • Current research consensus for this project: data correctness and benchmark quality are likely to matter at least as much as architectural novelty. papers.ssrn.com+2papers.ssrn.com+2

2. What the project is, academically

2.1 Core research framing

Academically, this project belongs at the intersection of:

  • financial forecasting

  • financial NLP

  • multimodal learning

  • multi-horizon time-series forecasting

  • out-of-sample model evaluation under temporal dependence

The strongest defensible formulation is not “predict stock prices,” but rather:

Learn a function that maps end-of-day market context and an as-of-close aggregated news state into horizon-specific outputs such as future returns, excess/abnormal returns, directional probabilities, downside-risk probabilities, or uncertainty-aware forecasts.

That framing is much stronger than raw price prediction because price levels are non-stationary and scale-sensitive, while return-like or rank-like objectives are more aligned with how forecasting quality is usually interpreted in empirical finance and predictive modeling. The project’s own benchmark-design notes already push in that direction by centering returns, abnormal/excess returns, direction, downside risk, ranking, and uncertainty rather than price levels.

2.2 Why “event state” is the right conceptual abstraction

The project’s theoretical shift away from “single-news impact” toward “event state” is strong. Classical event-study methodology is useful when a researcher can identify a reasonably clean event window and ask whether an announcement moved prices abnormally around that event. But event studies become much weaker when many overlapping narratives, confounds, repeated coverage cycles, sector spillovers, and after-hours publication effects all interact. MacKinlay’s classic review is still the canonical reference for the event-study logic and its complications. In your project, the right lesson to borrow is not “run event studies,” but “recognize how hard clean causal attribution becomes when events are overlapping and noisy.” That is exactly why your event-state framing is defensible. econpapers.repec.org

So the event-state idea should be interpreted as:

  • not a causal claim,

  • not a one-headline trigger detector,

  • but a representation of the recent information environment around a company.

That is a meaningful and mature research stance.

2.3 Why multimodality is justified

The project is multimodal in a genuinely natural way:

  • structured market time series capture realized market dynamics,

  • news text captures exogenous narrative and attention effects,

  • optional company/profile/fundamental context captures slower-moving priors.

This matches the current multimodal-finance literature, which increasingly treats market forecasting as a fusion problem among structured time series, text, and sometimes relational or contextual data. Recent survey work in financial multimodal modeling explicitly identifies the main recurring challenges as temporal misalignment, missing/noisy modalities, modality imbalance, and weak cross-regime generalization. Those are exactly the right theoretical warnings for your project. ScienceDirect+1

3. Current repository-backed project state

From the project materials and current internal scaffolding assumptions, the research now appears to rest on the following structure:

3.1 What the project seems to already support conceptually

The current project state assumes first-pass support for:

That means the project is no longer in the “blank repository” phase. The key question is no longer “what should the repo contain?” but rather:

Which research branches are mature enough to strengthen now, and which are too early, too fragile, or too expensive relative to their likely gain?

3.2 What the governance documents imply

The governance documents also make clear that the project now treats benchmark comparability as a first-class concern. The design/governance layer explicitly says benchmark methodology changes, target-definition changes, split-adjustment changes, and architecture changes must trigger benchmark invalidation review. That is a very strong sign that the project has already moved toward a serious research posture rather than casual experimentation.

This matters because it changes what “progress” means. In this project, progress is not just “higher score”; it is:

  • higher score with valid comparison,

  • under stable benchmark conditions,

  • with evidence that prior results remain comparable.

That is unusually mature for a Master’s project, and worth preserving.

4. Theoretical background: concepts that now define the project

4.1 Multi-horizon forecasting

A central concept in the project is that 1-day, 5-day, 20-day, and 60-day horizons are not interchangeable tasks. They may share information, but they are driven by different mechanisms:

  • 1-day horizons are more vulnerable to market microstructure noise, publication timing, and immediate sentiment reaction.

  • 5-day horizons may capture short persistence and delayed digestion.

  • 20-day horizons begin to resemble medium-term repricing.

  • 60-day horizons may benefit more from company-context, macro regime, or persistent narratives than from very short-term noise.

This is one reason why multi-output / horizon-specific architectures are appealing. Temporal Fusion Transformers are especially relevant here, not because the project must copy TFT, but because TFT formalized a strong modern view of multi-horizon forecasting with mixed input types, horizon-specific outputs, gating, and interpretable feature relevance. 4.2 Finance-specific text modeling

The project’s decision to use a finance-aware text representation is well supported. FinBERT and related finance-domain language models exist precisely because general-domain sentiment models miss the vocabulary, polarity shifts, and contextual semantics of finance. FinBERT is therefore a very sensible conceptual anchor for headline/sentence encoding or sentiment extraction. huggingface.co+1

That does not automatically mean “use FinBERT sentiment as the final model.” The stronger lesson is:

  • domain-adapted language representations matter,

  • but how those representations are aggregated temporally may matter more than the mere choice of encoder.

4.3 Multimodal fusion

The project’s fusion question is now central. The literature suggests three broad families:

  • early fusion: concatenate modalities before deeper modeling,

  • intermediate fusion: separate encoders then fuse latent representations,

  • late fusion: separate predictors then combine outputs.

The current research surrounding your project strongly points toward intermediate fusion as the most thesis-appropriate family, because it preserves modularity while allowing learned cross-modal interaction. Recent multimodal forecasting work combining market time series with news also leans in this direction. link.springer.com+1

4.4 Event studies vs event-state forecasting

This is worth emphasizing separately. Event-study logic and event-state forecasting are related, but they answer different questions:

  • event studies ask: what happened around a clean event?

  • event-state forecasting asks: what is the predictive value of the recent informational environment?

Your project is firmly in the second category. That is a more realistic framing for continuous news flow, but it also means you should be careful not to overclaim causal interpretation. MacKinlay is the right “conceptual contrast” citation here, not because you are doing a classical event study, but because his framework clarifies why the clean-event assumptions break down so quickly. econpapers.repec.org

If price histories are not properly adjusted, then multi-horizon returns, labels, error metrics, and ranking outputs can all be corrupted by artificial mechanical jumps.   • market close timestamp,

  • trading calendar alignment,

  • and next-trading-day assignment when necessary.

This is one of the most common silent leak channels in financial NLP forecasting. Your own benchmark framing already implicitly recognizes it by insisting on strict temporal causality.

5.3 Raw returns vs abnormal returns

One of the most important unresolved theoretical choices is whether the project should primarily model:

  • raw future returns,

  • abnormal/excess returns,

  • direction,

  • downside risk,

  • ranking,

  • or uncertainty.

At this stage, the strongest academic summary is:

  • raw returns are the most intuitive target but often the noisiest,

  • abnormal/excess returns may be more aligned with the “incremental information value” of news,

  • direction is easier to explain but may discard useful magnitude information,

  • downside risk is highly defensible if the project shifts toward risk-aware forecasting,

  • ranking may be the strongest way to show practical ordering skill even when point-error metrics look mediocre,

  • uncertainty outputs are scientifically valuable but usually secondary to getting the mean/rank task right.

That framing is also consistent with the project’s benchmark materials, which explicitly keep all of these task families in play and ask whether a model can be weak on RMSE but still useful on ranking.

6. Model architecture: current best interpretation

6.1 The likely current core architecture

Given the materials, the current working architecture can be summarized as:

  • market branch: daily OHLCV-derived features and rolling market context,

  • news branch: temporally aggregated event-state representation,

  • fusion layer: current first-pass multimodal model,

  • multi-horizon outputs: likely horizon-specific labels and at least first-pass support for multi-output evaluation.

That is already a coherent thesis architecture.

6.2 The strongest theoretical next-step architecture

The current research around the repository converged on a strong conclusion:

  • the single best next move is probably not a giant architecture jump,

  • but rather strengthening the current architecture with data-correctness and benchmark-correctness upgrades first,

  • followed by one carefully controlled architectural extension at a time.

That is a research-strength decision, not a conservative one. It reflects the fact that in finance, architecture can very easily overtake the quality of the targets and evaluation scheme.

6.3 Mixture of Experts as a future possibility

The project has also seriously entertained a Mixture-of-Experts path. The current research state treats it as interesting for modularity, but likely too complex and too hard to benchmark fairly as the immediate next step. The strongest interpretation of the current state is that MoE remains an extension candidate, not the current center of gravity. The present repo seems more naturally suited to incremental modular branches than to a full expert-routing redesign.

7. Benchmarking: the project’s methodological backbone

7.1 Why benchmarking now matters as much as modeling

The benchmark-research materials make one thing very clear: for this project, benchmarking is no longer an appendix. It is part of the scientific claim itself. The benchmark design is expected to cover:

  • regression,

  • classification,

  • ranking,

  • calibration,

  • multiple horizon types,

  • and tournament-style comparison of benchmark protocols.

7.2 The strongest current benchmark philosophy

The strongest current benchmark stance for the project is:

  • rolling / expanding walk-forward validation for development,

  • purge / embargo to handle overlapping forward labels,

  • a final recent untouched lockbox holdout for the last claim,

  • and task-appropriate metrics rather than one universal metric.

This is very consistent with financial ML best practice. López de Prado’s framework and the later PBO / CSCV literature are relevant because they explicitly attack the weaknesses of naive holdout/backtest evaluation in finance, especially when many model variants are explored. papers.ssrn.com+1

7.3 Forecast comparison and probabilistic evaluation

Two benchmark references are especially important for the thesis:

  • Diebold–Mariano for forecast-comparison logic when you want to compare predictive accuracy across competing models. tandfonline.com+1

  • Gneiting–Raftery for proper scoring rules when the project enters probabilistic or uncertainty-aware forecasting. tandfonline.com+1

These should not be treated as “fancy extras”; they are the theoretical foundation for claiming that one forecasting system really outperforms another, especially once uncertainty outputs enter the picture.

8. Current best research conclusions, structurally

8.1 What is strongest right now

The strongest elements of the project right now are:

  1. The problem framing is good.
    It is no longer a naive stock-price predictor. It is a well-formed multimodal, multi-horizon, EOD forecasting thesis concept.

  2. The event-state framing is defensible.
    It avoids the weak one-article-one-impact assumption and aligns better with continuous-news reality. econpapers.repec.org+1

  3. The benchmark awareness is unusually strong.
    The project is already treating benchmark comparability, split policy, invalidation, and fairness as governed objects, not afterthoughts.

  4. The repository appears broad enough for meaningful modular extensions.
    Not proven mature, but broad enough that the next steps can be chosen strategically rather than from scratch.

8.2 What is still weakest

The weakest parts, conceptually, are likely:

  1. split/corporate-action correctness is still not something to take for granted,

  2. target design is probably still more important than architecture complexity,

  3. the project can still drift into scope explosion if it adds too many branches too fast,

  4. MoE and some auxiliary modalities are more intellectually attractive than currently justified,

  5. the benchmark design must become the project’s stable backbone before major architecture expansion. papers.ssrn.com+1

9. Recommended structural summary of the project, today

If I had to summarize the current theoretical background of the project in one thesis-ready structure, I would write it like this:

A. Scientific motivation

Financial forecasting benefits from combining heterogeneous information sources because markets respond not only to realized time-series dynamics but also to external narrative information, firm context, and broader regimes. Multimodal models are therefore justified, but they are fragile unless temporal alignment, modality balance, and evaluation rigor are handled carefully. ScienceDirect+1

B. Core research question

Does a temporally aggregated event-state representation built from recent company news improve horizon-specific forecasting performance relative to market-only baselines, under leakage-aware end-of-day evaluation?

C. Core modalities

  • Daily market data

  • Timestamped company news

  • Optional company/fundamental/context priors

D. Core tasks

  • Return forecasting

  • Abnormal/excess return forecasting

  • Direction

  • Downside risk

  • Possibly uncertainty

  • Potentially cross-sectional ranking as a more defensible primary benchmark than point-value error alone

E. Core implementation logic

  • immutable raw/interim/final data layering

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • split/corporate-action correction

  • modular feature branches

  • modular model branches

  • multi-horizon outputs

  • reproducible run and evaluation structure

F. Core benchmark logic

  • walk-forward temporal validation

  • purge/embargo where overlap matters

  • final lockbox recent holdout

  • task-appropriate metrics

  • formal forecast-comparison logic where relevant

  • careful treatment of benchmark invalidation when targets or data contracts change

G. Core research risk

The main risk is no longer “will the model converge?” but rather:

will the project make a strong, clean, defensible claim that survives scrutiny on targets, data timing, corporate actions, and fair out-of-sample comparison?
